title: Retrouvailles au Grand Colbert  (Reunion at Grand Colbert)

segments.t: At Le Grand Colbert restaurant, Mathias finally arrives to meet Annick and their daughter Camille. Years of estrangement create palpable tension as the former couple exchange polite pleasantries and order drinks. Listen to the conversation in French first.
J'ai besoin d'un verre. Garçon!
Regarde maman, il est là.
Il n'a pas changé.
Toi non plus.
Bonjour Annick. Bonjour Camille.
Bonjour Mathias.
Vous n'allez pas vous serrer la main?
Non, bien sûr que non.
Asseyez-vous, Mathias.
Un homme important doit être pressé.
Oh, vous savez...
Juste un café, s'il vous plaît.
Et un verre de rouge pour moi.
Je m'en occupe.
Vous vous occupez de tout, toujours.
Mieux vaut tard que jamais.
Let's walk through the conversation step by step.
J'ai besoin d'un verre. Garçon!
'I need a drink. Waiter!' Ordering 'a glass' means 'a drink' in French, followed by a classic brasserie call that literally means 'boy!' for a waiter.
Regarde maman, il est là.
'Look Mom, he is here.' Dropping the final '-s' on 'look' marks a casual command to one person, while the closing pointer covers both 'here' and 'there' in French.
Il n'a pas changé.
'He has not changed.' Wrapping 'has' inside the negative frame while leaving 'changed' outside is standard past order in French.
Toi non plus.
'Neither have you.' Literally 'you no more', this compact three-word expression is how you say 'neither do you' or 'me neither' after any negative remark.
Bonjour Annick. Bonjour Camille.
'Hello Annick. Hello Camille.' Repeating 'good day' before each person's first name individually is considered warm, attentive manners in French.
Bonjour Mathias.
'Hello Mathias.' Answering with the same polite 'good day' plus his first name keeps the greeting balanced without revealing too much warmth in French.
Vous n'allez pas vous serrer la main?
'Are you not going to shake hands?' Literally 'squeeze each other the hand', French uses 'the hand' in the singular where English says 'shake hands'.
Non, bien sûr que non.
'No, of course not.' Echoing 'no' at both ends of 'no, well sure that no' gives Mathias's refusal extra certainty in French.
Asseyez-vous, Mathias.
'Sit down, Mathias.' Switching from old intimacy to formal 'you' on 'sit yourself down' shows the guarded distance between Annick and Mathias in French.
Un homme important doit être pressé.
'An important man must be in a hurry.' Putting 'important' after 'man' follows normal order in French, paired with 'must be pressed' to mean 'must be in a rush'.
Oh, vous savez...
'Oh, you know...' Mathias mirrors Annick's formal 'you' in this handy phrase, trailing off modestly just like 'oh, you know...' in English.
Juste un café, s'il vous plaît.
'Just a coffee, please.' Addressing the waiter calls for the polite 'you' version of 'please'—literally 'if it pleases you'.
Et un verre de rouge pour moi.
'And a glass of red wine for me.' Cafe regulars drop 'wine' altogether and simply ask for 'a glass of red' in French.
Je m'en occupe.
'I will take care of it.' Slipping a tiny 'of it' marker ahead of 'occupy' builds a useful sentence you'll hear everywhere for 'I've got this'.
Vous vous occupez de tout, toujours.
'You take care of everything, always.' Hearing polite 'you' twice side by side sounds funny at first, because the first means 'you' and the second means 'yourself' in French.
Mieux vaut tard que jamais.

'Better late than never.' Built word-for-word as 'better is-worth late than never', this classic French proverb matches the English saying almost piece for piece. Now let's listen to the whole scene again at normal speed, and see how much more you catch.
J'ai besoin d'un verre. Garçon!
Regarde maman, il est là.
Il n'a pas changé.
Toi non plus.
Bonjour Annick. Bonjour Camille.
Bonjour Mathias.
Vous n'allez pas vous serrer la main?
Non, bien sûr que non.
Asseyez-vous, Mathias.
Un homme important doit être pressé.
Oh, vous savez...
Juste un café, s'il vous plaît.
Et un verre de rouge pour moi.
Je m'en occupe.
Vous vous occupez de tout, toujours.
Mieux vaut tard que jamais.

Mathias and Annick attempt to bridge eight years of distance over coffee and wine, under the watchful gaze of their daughter Camille. Listen to the French conversation one more time. See you next time!
Au revoir!
